title: The day two defects hid their own fixes, and the release lane stood still behind a dialog nobody could see
problem: The Queen could not see work filed after an epic's hundredth timeline event, dismissed every fix whose defect it could read, and - in the release lane - could do nothing at all, because a macOS keychain dialog had been waiting on screen since a rebuild. Each of the first two defects blocked the issue that described it.
findings: The epic timeline was read one page deep. Events arrive oldest-first, so the page that falls off holds the NEWEST cross-references. #1090 held 104 events; the highest issue visible was #1228, and three open issues did not exist as far as choosing was concerned while the journal said 'Nothing to choose from 19 candidates' for hours.

'looks already done' called work finished when every identifier its criteria named was present in the boundary files. For a FIX, those identifiers exist because the defect exists - #1288's criteria name fetchPullRequest because that function loses the status - so eight of seventeen candidates were dismissed before anyone could touch them. Gated now on evidence that postdates the issue: a boundary file with no commits since the issue was filed cannot hold its fix.

Both defects hid their own fixes. The issue asking the Queen to see past page one lay past page one; the issue describing the already-done heuristic named an identifier that made the heuristic dismiss it. Neither could be delegated; both had to be fixed by hand.

A keychain that times out on EVERY operation is a dialog, not a keychain. pgrep -x SecurityAgent named it in one command after two rounds of guessing. Three discriminators settle it: the shell reads the same service's attributes in 24 ms, the OTHER variant's app reads the same service successfully in the same minute, and the timing starts at a rebuild - a new ad-hoc signature no longer matches the ACL. Everything the release lane could not do traced there: dispatch, local-auth, conversation encryption, reconciliation.

The dev lane is the control that proves the code sound: same persistence code, file-based credentials instead of the keychain, ZERO plaintext fallbacks and zero plaintext reads across its whole log, while the release lane wrote 18 fallbacks and could re-encrypt none of them.

Housekeeping that only runs after thirty quiet minutes never runs. The archive sweep lives inside a report loop that sleeps first; four relaunches in an hour - all mine - meant no record was ever stamped, and the reconciliation went on calling settled work 'the work exists and nobody is looking at it'. One sweep at start fixed it: fourteen archive lines, stamps 48 to 62, and the next pass read 'zero disagree in a way that needs looking at' where the briefing had reported eight per tick.

A briefing whose criteria name files outside its boundary cannot be passed. I wrote two in one day. #1287 asked for a logic suite and permitted only ChatViewModel, so the bee put its suite inside ChatViewModel; #1288 asked for the poller, a drill and a suite and permitted only the client, so four of five criteria were unreachable and an exact change came back 1/5.

The bee out-did the brief twice. #1287 made the caught error a REQUIRED argument of the only emitter, so dropping it stops compiling; #1288 found the next defect while proving its own and named it in its own log line rather than papering over it.
fix: Paginate the epic timeline with a stopping rule and a bound. Gate the already-done heuristic on evidence that postdates the issue. Detect a waiting SecurityAgent after a failed warm-up cycle and say whether retrying can help. Archive once at start, before the loop's first sleep. Judge the pull-request guard by the branch's named commit rather than the last turn's file count. Fall back to the vendored QueenUILib halves when the shared checkout loses its build map mid-compile. Keep the caught error in queen.pr.poll_failed and the HTTP status in a decode failure.
prevention: When a defect describes the machinery that would find its own issue, do not delegate it - the delegation path is the thing that is broken.
A refusal you cannot find is usually under a key you did not grep: '/accept' logs queen.accept.blocked, and I called it silent twice.
open --env applies only at launch. Kill, VERIFY dead with pgrep, then open - a watchdog can restart the app between the two.
Every file the criteria touch must be inside the boundary. Written into the new queen-briefing skill with both instances.
Cheap proxies for 'did this land' failed twice: commit messages cite issue numbers in prose, and Closes #N is not reliably written even though L1 requires it. The honest measurement was the date.
corrections_to_earlier_claims: I reported a gate green that was red: 'cmd; echo exit=$?' swallowed make's exit code. Every gate run now reports REAL_EXIT.
I said prNumber was not recorded. The field is pullRequestNumber and it was recorded all along; I read a name that does not exist and called the None a defect.
I predicted the reconcile count would fall after dismissing records. It rose, 4 to 6, because the gate reads the archive stamp rather than the state.
I suspected my own pagination of starving the keychain. Measured: no choose pass had run since that relaunch, so those reads never happened.
